prerequisites: Previous knowledge of Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics is essential, having taken the corresponding subjects. It is also highly recommended to have previously taken the subject Thermal Machines or an analogous subject dealing with power cycles (especially the Joule/Brayton and Otto and Diesel cycles).

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge and ability to apply the scientific and technological fundamentals of internal combustion engines.

syllabus_topics: Block I. Reciprocating Internal Combustion Engines
Topic 1. GENERALITIES OF RECIPROCATING INTERNAL COMBUSTION ENGINES
Components and basic processes of a reciprocating internal combustion engine.
Classification of RICE according to various criteria.
Evolution of the working fluid during engine operation (p-V diagram and indicator diagram).
Equivalent air cycles of constant volume combustion and limited pressure.
Topic 2. THE COMBUSTION PROCESS IN SPARK-IGNITION ENGINES AND COMPRESSION-IGNITION ENGINES
Types of combustion in reciprocating internal combustion engines.
Normal and abnormal combustion in SI engines (detonation and surface ignition).
Combustion in CI engines: main functions of injection in CI engines (micromixing and macromixing), combustion phases and influence of different factors.
Other types of combustion in RICE: dual-fuel engines, stratified charge engines, HCCI combustion engines.
Topic 3. HEAT LOSSES AND COOLING. MECHANICAL LOSSES AND LUBRICATION
Location and importance of heat losses in RICE.
General heat transfer equations applied to the engine.
Engine thermal balance.
Cooling systems, principles and comparative analysis: Air and water cooling.
Classification of mechanical losses.
Analysis of factors affecting friction losses.
Analysis of factors affecting pumping losses.
Systems used for engine lubrication; principles and comparative analysis.
Topic 4. CHARGE RENEWAL IN TWO-STROKE AND FOUR-STROKE ENGINES
Principles of charge renewal in 4-stroke engines and parameters to characterize this process.
Identification of main factors affecting charge renewal in 4-stroke engines.
Principles of charge renewal in 2-stroke engines and parameters to characterize this process.
Identification of main factors affecting charge renewal in 2-stroke engines.
Topic 5. MIXTURE FORMATION IN SI AND CI ENGINES
Considerations on mixture requirements in SI engines.
Equipment for mixture formation in SI engines.
Injection in CI engines.
Block II. Aviation Gas Turbines
Topic 6. JET ENGINES I
Classification of jet engines.
Thrust generation in jet engines: air-breathing jets and rocket engines.
Working cycle of turbojets, thermodynamic evolution of the fluid in the different components of the engine.
Analysis of convergent nozzle choking.
Definition of turbojet efficiencies.
Optimal parameters of the turbojet thermodynamic cycle.
Topic 7. JET ENGINES II
The turbofan: mechanical scheme and analysis of the working cycles of the primary and secondary flows, advantages over the turbojet.
The turboprop.
Fields of application and design trends of aviation gas turbines.
Topic 8. JET ENGINES III
Characteristics of the gas generator.
Characteristic curves of the turbomachinery of the gas generator: compressor and turbine.
Basic notions on off-design operation of an aviation gas turbine.
Equilibrium operating line of the gas generator.
Justification for the use of two or three-spool configurations, compressor bleed, and variable geometry compressor.
Topic 9. JET ENGINES IV
Additional information on characteristics of aviation gas turbine components: subsonic and supersonic dynamic inlets, convergent-divergent propulsive nozzles.
Variable geometry nozzles.
Principle of afterburning.
teaching_methods: Distance learning supported by Information and Communication Technologies (ICT).
Self-study with specially designed basic bibliography including solved exercises and self-assessment tests.
Voluntary continuous assessment tests (PECs) with practical exercises using virtual software or spreadsheets.
In-person practical sessions to interact with real materials and equipment.
Interaction with teaching staff, tutors, and peers through virtual course forums and web conferences.
assessment_rules: The final grade is calculated as: In-person exam grade + 0.1 * Average PEC grade + 0.5 points for practices. To pass, students must achieve a weighted average grade of 5/10 or higher, obtain at least 5/10 in the theoretical part of the in-person exam, and at least 3/10 in the problem part. Mandatory attendance and passing of in-person laboratory practices are required to pass the course. The PECs and practices can increase the final grade, but only if the minimum requirements for the in-person exam are met (the PEC increment is capped at 10% of the exam grade, and the practice increment of 0.5 points requires a grade of >=7/10 in the practice evaluation).
